meta.description: Not Augustine. Wikiquote lists it as misattributed; it likely rewords Oscar Wilde's 1893 epigram, first seen this way in Ahmad Sohrab's Persian Rosary (c. 1929).
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no saint without a past, no sinner without a future'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Augustine. The line likely rewords Oscar Wilde's 1893 epigram ('every saint has a past'); this form is earliest known from Ahmad Sohrab's Persian Rosary (c. 1929).

answer.label: Not Augustine of Hippo — likely a rewording of Oscar Wilde
answer.sourceLine: No work of Augustine’s contains this line. Wikiquote ↗ lists it under Misattributed and gives its earliest known appearance as Ahmad Sohrab’s Persian Rosary (c. 1929). Wikiquote says it is probably a paraphrase of Lord Illingworth’s epigram in Wilde’s A Woman of No Importance, first staged in 1893: “every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.”

source.heading: Where the idea actually comes from

docMeta.dd: Earliest known: Ahmad Sohrab, A Persian Rosary (c. 1929, per Wikiquote)

source.excerpt:
LADY HUNSTANTON. … I have a dim idea, dear Lord Illingworth, that you are always on the side of the sinners, and I know I always try to be on the side of the saints, but that is as far as I get. And after all, it may be merely the fancy of a drowning person.

LORD ILLINGWORTH. The only difference between the saint and the sinner is that every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.
trail: Wikiquote, Augustine of Hippo ↗ lists the line under Misattributed. It gives Ahmad Sohrab’s Persian Rosary (c. 1929) as the earliest known occurrence, probably paraphrasing Wilde’s 1893 play.

Wilde’s epigram, spoken by Lord Illingworth in the Third Act of A Woman of No Importance, is in the Project Gutenberg text ↗. Its front matter records the Haymarket premiere of 19 April 1893 and a first printing in 1894.
An archived scan of Sohrab’s undated typescript, “A Persian Rosary” ↗, has as item 5: “There is no saint without a past. There is no sinner without a future.”

Pope Francis used the line in his Santa Marta homily of 19 January 2016. The Vatican’s summary of the homily ↗ quotes him: “there are no saints without a past, nor sinners without a future.” He credits no one.
source.excerptNote: Wilde wrote a cynical joke: a saint is someone whose sins are behind them. The popular version turns it into a statement of hope. Its two-clause “no saint without a past / no sinner without a future” form first appears, as far as is known, in item 5 of Ahmad Sohrab’s typescript A Persian Rosary: “There is no saint without a past. There is no sinner without a future.”

sourceLink.text: A Woman of No Importance, full text (Project Gutenberg)

source.rightsNote: The popular wording goes back only to Ahmad Sohrab’s Persian Rosary. Wikiquote dates it c. 1929, but the surviving typescript scan carries no date, and WIST notes that the edition dates are unclear, so we assert no copyright status for that wording. Wilde’s original sentence, from a play first printed in 1894, is in the US public domain.

author.name: Oscar Wilde
author.heading: The wit behind the line
author.bio: Oscar Wilde was the Dublin-born playwright of Lady Windermere’s Fan, A Woman of No Importance and The Importance of Being Earnest, and was famous for epigrams that turn moral commonplaces upside down. In A Woman of No Importance, which opened at the Haymarket Theatre in London on 19 April 1893, the cynical Lord Illingworth says that “every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.” The “no saint without a past” line now credited to Augustine is most likely a later rewording of that joke.

misattribution.heading: Why Augustine gets the credit
misattribution.intro: The line suits Augustine’s story of a sinful youth followed by conversion, which is probably why it attached to him. But no one has found it in any of his writings, and the specialists file it as misattributed.

items.scope: Popular attribution on quote sites and social media
items.why: Wikiquote ↗ says the line is “sometimes attributed to Augustine”. It places it in its Misattributed section, with Sohrab’s Persian Rosary (c. 1929) as the earliest known occurrence.

items.scope: Earliest known source of this exact two-clause form
items.why: Sohrab (1890–1958) was a Persian-American Bahá’í writer, and the line appears in his maxim list “A Persian Rosary” ↗. WIST ↗ credits the wording to him and says it found no evidence he borrowed it from Wilde. Wikiquote calls it probably a Wilde paraphrase. The sources disagree on that point.
He used the line in his 19 January 2016 homily ↗ as his own reflection on King David, with no attribution. He did not originate it.

misattribution.truthLine: The idea goes back at least to Oscar Wilde’s A Woman of No Importance (first staged 1893). There Lord Illingworth says “every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future” (Project Gutenberg ↗). The “no saint without a past” form is a later rewording, earliest known from Ahmad Sohrab’s Persian Rosary.

context.heading: From a drawing-room joke to a sermon line
lead: In Wilde’s play the line is a jab from a worldly aristocrat. Lord Illingworth uses it to tease Lady Hunstanton, who has just admitted she always tries to be “on the side of the saints.” The point is cynical: saints are simply sinners whose sins are behind them.

Recast as “There is no saint without a past, no sinner without a future,” the same reversal becomes a message of hope and redemption. In that form it travels easily in religious settings, attaches to Augustine, the best-known reformed sinner among the saints, and was used by Pope Francis in a 2016 homily.
context.pull: Every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.

schema.verdictNote: Commonly misattributed to Augustine of Hippo. The popular wording 'There is no saint without a past, no sinner without a future' is earliest known from Ahmad Sohrab's A Persian Rosary (c. 1929) and is probably a later paraphrase of Oscar Wilde's 1893 line quoted here; WIST finds no evidence that Sohrab borrowed it from Wilde.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's Augustine page lists 'There is no saint without a past, no sinner without a future' under Misattributed, says it is sometimes attributed to Augustine, gives Ahmad Sohrab's Persian Rosary (c. 1929) as the earliest known occurrence, and calls it probably a paraphrase of Wilde's 1893 A Woman of No Importance.

In A Woman of No Importance, Third Act, Lord Illingworth says: 'The only difference between the saint and the sinner is that every saint has a past, and every sinner has a future.' Front matter: Haymarket Theatre, 19 April 1893; first printed 1894; Methuen 8th edition 1919.
Typescript 'A Persian Rosary, By Mirza Ahmad Sohrab', item 5: 'There is no saint without a past. There is no sinner without a future.' (scan bears no date)

WIST credits the quote to Mirza Ahmad Sohrab (1890–1958), A Persian Rosary of Nineteen Pearls (1929), says edition dates are unclear, notes the Augustine misattribution, and found no evidence Sohrab borrowed it from Wilde.
Pope Francis, Santa Marta morning meditation, 19 January 2016 ('Saint and sinner'): 'there are no saints without a past, nor sinners without a future', not attributed to anyone.
